clue.text: Careless friends overturned barrel (8)

indicators.note: turned upside down, so the word reads backwards

blocks.note: pals = friends
to barrel along = to dash, move very fast

explanation.surface: A drunken mishap: someone's careless mates have knocked over a barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barrel' looks like a noun, a cask the friends tipped over; it is the verb, to rush.
explanation.definitionFit: Slapdash work is done hastily and carelessly.

clue.text: Knight’s destiny attached to weapon (8)

indicators.note: fixed on to the end of, so LOT follows LANCE

blocks.note: a lance is a knight's long spear
one's lot = one's fate

explanation.surface: A knight's fate is bound up with the lance he carries.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s is short for 'is', not a possessive: the knight equals what follows, rather than owning a destiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Lancelot is the most famous knight of the Round Table.

clue.text: Frenchman eats fruit in apartment (4-1-5)

indicators.note: a word that eats another takes it inside itself

blocks.note: Pierre, a typical French first name
a date is a fruit of the palm; it goes in after PIE

explanation.surface: A Frenchman snacks on fruit at home in his flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eats' is the container signal, not a meal; the enumeration's hyphens show a borrowed French phrase, literally 'foot on the ground'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pied-à-terre is a small flat kept for occasional use, often in a city.

clue.text: Cost of moving song about boring argument (3,7)

indicators.note: boring into something means drilling inside it

blocks.note: an air is a tune or song
a fight = a quarrel
re = about, concerning; it goes in after F

explanation.surface: A tune about a dull quarrel over the cost of a house move.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like 'dull', describing the argument; it is the verb, drilling RE into FIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Air freight is the charge for sending goods by air, as well as the goods themselves.

clue.text: Henry always left mature food for cattle (7)

blocks.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
ay (or aye) = always, an old and Scots word
L = left
to age = to mature

explanation.surface: A man called Henry has always left food to ripen for his cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: AY for 'always' is old-fashioned, as in 'for ay and ay'. Haylage sits between hay and silage: grass partly dried, then sealed.
explanation.definitionFit: Haylage is partly dried grass stored airtight as fodder for livestock.

clue.text: Old film star’s short dress (4)

indicators.note: cut short, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: Greta GARBO, Hollywood star of the 1920s and 30s, loses her O

explanation.surface: A remark on the skimpy frock worn by a screen star of yesteryear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short dress' reads as a mini; 'short' works on the star's name, and 'dress' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Garb is clothing, dress in the general sense.

clue.text: Back to suppress introduction of rude language (6)

indicators.note: to keep something held down inside
the first letter of the next word

blocks.note: to back a horse = to bet on it
first letter of 'rude', held inside after B

explanation.surface: A call to push back and stop crude talk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' is the wordplay here, not a direction: BET ON, with R squeezed in after the B.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the Celtic tongue spoken in Brittany, north-west France, is one of many languages.

clue.text: I don’t know a silly thing to say at customs? (6,2)

definitions.text: a silly thing to say at customs?

blocks.note: the everyday shrug of a reply

blocks.clueFragment: a silly thing to say at customs?
blocks.note: the same words taken literally, as an invitation to an officer

explanation.surface: A shrugging reply that would be unwise in front of a border officer.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition takes the phrase literally: invite a customs officer to search you and they may well do it.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Search me' is an idiom meaning 'I have no idea'.

clue.text: Area recently allowing in vehicle with choice of fare (1,2,5)

indicators.note: letting something come inside

blocks.note: A = area
late = recently, as in 'of late'
a car is a vehicle; it goes in after LA

explanation.surface: A local area has lately started letting in a car that offers a menu.
explanation.walkthrough: A + LA(CAR)TE. 'Fare' is food here, not the price of a ride, despite the vehicle nearby.
explanation.definitionFit: À la carte dining lets you choose individual dishes from the menu.

clue.text: Working group joining meetING EARlier (2,4)

indicators.note: letters grouped across the join of two words

blocks.note: the end of 'meeting' plus the start of 'earlier'

explanation.surface: A working group joining a meeting that started earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals give the answer away; 'Working group' reads as one committee, but 'Working' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom comes from machinery: with the gears engaged the engine drives, so the phrase means functioning properly.

clue.text: Movie about criminals chasing outspoken feisty woman: Kill Bill? (10)

indicators.note: said out loud, so go by sound
coming after, so BUSTER goes second

blocks.note: a filly is a lively young woman
Buster (1988) is a film about the Great Train Robbery

explanation.surface: A film review: a crime movie, a spirited heroine, and Tarantino's revenge film.
explanation.walkthrough: Kill Bill is a Tarantino film, which the surface leans on; here it means kill a parliamentary bill by talking it out.
explanation.definitionFit: A filibuster is a marathon speech used to stop a bill passing, so it can kill a bill.

clue.text: Able to swallow large fly (4)

indicators.note: to swallow is to take food down inside you, so one word goes inside another

blocks.note: fit = able, capable
L = large, the clothing size; it goes in after F

explanation.surface: A boast that one could gulp down a big insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fly' looks like the insect being swallowed; it is the verb, to dart about.
explanation.definitionFit: To flit is to fly lightly and quickly from place to place.

clue.text: Snarled “Get in the hole!” after draining final putt here? (10)

indicators.note: tangled, so the letters are mixed up
emptying a word of its middle letters

blocks.note: taken as it is
HOLE drained of its inside letters OL

explanation.surface: A golfer growls at the ball as it drops for the last putt of the round.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue works as a picture of the answer: the final putt on a course is sunk on the eighteenth green, which bloggers call a semi-&lit.
explanation.definitionFit: A golf round has eighteen holes, so the last putt goes in at the eighteenth.

clue.text: In Calais, very old hat beginning to rile intruder? (10)

blocks.note: très is French for 'very'
passé = out of date, old hat
first letter of 'rile'

explanation.surface: In a French port, an outdated hat starts to annoy someone who has barged in.
explanation.walkthrough: Calais is the French port; 'In Calais' means translate into French. 'Old hat' is an idiom, not headwear.
explanation.definitionFit: A trespasser is someone who intrudes on another's land.

clue.text: Flat-hunter might go here, surprisingly leasing a flat with floor missing (4,6)

indicators.note: in an unexpected form, so the letters are rearranged
FL, the abbreviation for floor, is taken away

blocks.note: taken as it is
A, then FLAT without FL (floor)

explanation.surface: Someone looking for a flat to rent might be surprised to lease one with no floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat-hunter' looks like a house-hunter; it is someone who wants flat country. East Anglia, the eastern bulge of England around Norfolk and Suffolk, is famously flat.
explanation.definitionFit: East Anglia, with the Fens, is the flattest region of England, a fair place to seek flat land.

clue.text: Art goes off in repository (7)

indicators.note: gone bad, so the letters are spoiled into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: Artworks are being sent off into a store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' reads as the art being sent away; it means spoiled, the way milk goes off.
explanation.definitionFit: A repository is a place where things are kept: storage.

clue.text: Rigid small boat delivered (8)

blocks.note: S = small
a tub is a slow, clumsy boat
a baby delivered is born

explanation.surface: A stiff little boat has been dropped off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivered' suggests a package; it means brought into the world.
explanation.definitionFit: Stubborn means unbending, rigid in one's views.

clue.text: Rest of money in Bucharest? Certainly (7)

blocks.note: lei is the plural of leu, Romania's currency
sure = certainly, as a reply

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the rest of the money is in Bucharest, and gets a yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rest of money' reads as the remainder of the cash; 'Rest' is the definition, a break.
explanation.definitionFit: Leisure is free time, rest from work.

clue.text: Again do something naughty, on and off, before death (8)

indicators.note: placed ahead of the next piece

blocks.note: re = on, concerning
taken as it is
death = the end

explanation.surface: Someone keeps misbehaving, now and then, until they die.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On and off' looks like 'intermittently'; each word is a separate piece, and 'on' becomes RE.
explanation.definitionFit: To reoffend is to commit another crime.

clue.text: Augment supply for life-changing substance (7)

indicators.note: the adverb of supple, flexibly, so the letters bend into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

explanation.surface: A call to boost the supply of a drug that transforms lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a noun meaning stock; read it as supp-ly, supplely.
explanation.definitionFit: A mutagen alters DNA, changing living things, which makes 'life-changing' a literal fit.

clue.text: The state of America in 2025? The trick is to be elsewhere after this (10)

definitions.text: The trick is to be elsewhere after this

blocks.note: Donald Trump became US president again in January 2025

blocks.clueFragment: The trick is to be elsewhere after this
blocks.note: a card-play term from bridge and whist

explanation.surface: A political wisecrack about the US in 2025, and a hint that the smart move is to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is from bridge or whist: to undertrump is to play a lower trump than one already played, so the trick goes to someone else.
explanation.definitionFit: America in 2025 was 'under Trump'; undertrumping hands the trick to another player.

clue.text: Formulate wordplay for “charge”? (4,2)

indicators.note: the clue asks for a recipe rather than a result, so the answer is the instructions that lead to 'charge'

blocks.note: a ward is a charge, someone in another's care; the recipe spells it backwards
in a down entry, 'up' is the instruction to read a word backwards

explanation.surface: A request to devise a cryptic clue for the word 'charge'.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: the answer's words are themselves the recipe. In a down entry 'up' means reversed, so DRAW up is WARD.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb comes from drafting documents: you set down the terms of a contract or plan in writing.

clue.text: Insomnia periodically to return soon (4)

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter
going back, so read right to left

blocks.note: the even-placed letters of iNsOmNiA, taken in order

explanation.surface: Someone hoping their sleepless nights will come back only now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Periodically' picks every other letter; 'to return' turns them round. Anon is old-fashioned, as in Shakespeare's 'I come anon'.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is an old word for soon, in a little while.

clue.text: Certainly ban smelly American drunk (2,3,5)

indicators.note: reeling, so the letters stagger into a new order

blocks.note: taken as it is
A = American

explanation.surface: A hearty yes to barring a pungent, drunken American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' looks like the American's state; it tells you to rearrange, and 'smelly' is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: 'By all means' is an emphatic 'certainly'.

clue.text: Greeted Zulu in French city (4)

blocks.note: met = greeted on arrival
Zulu is Z in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: A Zulu was welcomed in a French town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greeted' is past tense, so MET rather than MEET; 'Zulu' looks like a person but is only a letter from the radio alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Metz is a city in north-eastern France.

clue.text: Metal plate, one covering front of Aga (6)

indicators.note: taking the place of, as a stand-in covers for someone

blocks.note: a salver is a flat serving tray
I = one, the Roman numeral
first letter of 'Aga'; I replaces it in SALVER

explanation.surface: A metal plate as a guard on the front of an Aga, the big British range cooker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Metal plate' reads as one thing, but 'Metal' is the definition and 'plate' the SALVER; 'covering' means standing in for, not lying over.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the answer is one of the precious metals, alongside gold and platinum.

clue.text: Way to protect grant for ball game? (8)

indicators.note: wrapping around something to keep it safe

blocks.note: a route = a way
to let = to allow, grant; it goes in after ROU

explanation.surface: Someone seeks a way to safeguard funding for a ball sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ball game' suggests football; roulette is a game played with a ball, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Roulette is a casino game in which a small ball settles in a numbered slot.

clue.text: On returning, amorous nurses married in historic duchy (8)

indicators.note: ON coming back, so read backwards
holds something, as a nurse holds a baby

blocks.note: taken as it is, then turned round
randy = lustful
M = married; it goes in after R

explanation.surface: A lustful pair heading back home, with a married couple, in old French lands.
explanation.walkthrough: NO + R(M)ANDY. 'Nurses' looks like the hospital staff; it is a verb, holding M.
explanation.definitionFit: Normandy was a medieval duchy, whose duke William conquered England in 1066.
